transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-10-07 16:00 PT | Duration: 54m | Attendees: Jordan Miller (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Ethan Park (Sierra CTO), Lina Gomez (ML Eng), Mark Rivers (Infra), Olga Ivanova (PM)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:05] Ethan: yeah loud and clear, thanks Jordan. appreciate you fitting us in.
[00:10] Jordan: cool so goal for today is to understand your migration from OpenAI, talk through Dedicated and Private options, and figure out next steps for a pilot and benchmarks. priya will jump into technical q's.
[00:21] Olga: quick note — timeline is kinda tight, we're looking to reduce per-token spend asap and also ensure latency for live chat is stable.
[00:29] Priya: great, Lina can you give a quick run-through of your workloads and current infra?
[00:34] Lina: sure, so primary workloads — conversational support bot (short prompts, low to mid token lengths, high qps), and a secondary batch summarization pipeline for long docs up to 8k tokens. right now all hosted on OpenAI for chat and some experimental vLLM clusters in-house for batch.
[00:50] Mark: to add, infra team runs k8s on GCP, we've tried TGI/vLLM for offline but stability and kv-cache persistence became a pain. we want predictable throughput with less engineering overhead.
[01:05] Priya: ok makes sense. are you using function calling heavily? any structured output constraints?
[01:10] Lina: function calling yes on chat, and for summarization we need faithful output and some hallucination constraints — we run evals with ROUGE + a custom factuality check.
[01:20] Jordan: perfect. on the migration question — most customers come to Redwood because they want predictable latency and unit-cost control and to avoid maintaining vLLM ops themselves. curious — what's pushing you off OpenAI?
[01:31] Ethan: primarily cost — as volume increased our monthly bills jumped. second is the desire for data residency and audit logs. And we'd like to own performance characteristics more — not get surprised by transient limits.
[01:44] Olga: also procurement wants proof we can meet SOC2 and support SSO + KMS.
[01:50] Priya: we do SOC2 and can integrate KMS; for Private deployments we give you control over network. that said, there's always tradeoffs: Dedicated offers reserved capacity with Redwood-managed GPUs, Private is more isolated but takes longer to deploy.
[02:05] Lina: technical q — how compatible are models and prompts? we use GPT-4-like models and a few open variants via OpenAI endpoint. will we get parity?
[02:15] Priya: good question. parity depends on model families and evals. Redwood hosts curated open models and can also serve customer-provided model binaries if licensure allows. performance and output parity often require evals: temp/decoding parameters, context window handling, and tokenization edge-cases. we usually run a head-to-head on your sample prompts.
[02:36] Ethan: what about vLLM/TGI — we run some in-house experiments with vLLM and TGI. any compatibility gotchas?
[02:44] Priya: vLLM/TGI are great but operationally they're heavy for 24/7 production. Redwood's runtime implements similar optimizations (kv cache, continuous batching, kernel selection) and supports models that vLLM/TGI run, but you'll want to validate quantization and kernel paths. sometimes you see slight distributional differences in generation, especially with quantized weights.
[03:05] Lina: ok so we should send you the prompts and expected metrics.
[03:08] Priya: yes, send representative prompt sets + golden outputs; we'll run eval parity and measure latency p50/p95 and cost per 1k tokens.
[03:18] Mark: on network — if we go Dedicated hosted by Redwood, is data in our VPC or do we need Private?
[03:24] Jordan: Dedicated is dedicated GPU pools but still in Redwood-managed network; Private (VPC or on-prem) gives you customer-controlled networking and is ideal for stricter residency/KMS needs.
[03:34] Mark: and what about logging and audit? we need full request/response audit logs retained for 90 days.
[03:40] Priya: we can enable audit logs and integrate with your SIEM; retention and export policies are configurable (we've done 90+ day retention for Enterprise customers).
[03:48] Olga: procurement will want a security pack (SOC2, ISO certs, pen test).
[03:52] Jordan: we'll send the security docs and checklist.
[03:55] Ethan: another concern — how do you handle fallback if capacity hits limits? we've seen OpenAI rate limits and degraded service.
[04:03] Priya: Redwood routes by policy; Dedicated has reserved capacity and can burst if configured. we also support automated fallback to smaller variants or different regions. our SLOs are SLA-backed for Dedicated plans.
[04:15] Lina: what about model versioning and rollouts? we want canarying for new models.
[04:20] Priya: Redwood Console supports canary rollouts, A/B tests, and automatic fallback. you can pin model versions and stage traffic.
[04:28] Olga: cost — can you give a rough delta vs OpenAI?
[04:31] Jordan: depends on workload and batching. ballpark, customers migrating see 40-70% reduction in unit cost for token generation when using Dedicated with optimized batching and quantization, but we should run numbers on your actual prompts.
[04:45] Ethan: that aligns with our goal. for evals, we run both quality and latency — so we'll need Redwood to measure p50/p95 and also end-to-end app-level latency with our pre/post-processing.
[04:58] Priya: we'll instrument both sides in the pilot; we provide tracing hooks and token-level breakdowns in the Console. also we'll surface where batching helps versus when low-latency single-token responses are needed.
[05:12] Lina: one more — for long-context summarization, does your runtime support 8k+ windows and do you have recommendations on kv-cache persistence?
[05:21] Priya: yes; runtime supports long contexts up to 32k depending on model; kv-cache handling and kernel selection are tuned automatically. for large summaries we often recommend batching and prefix caching to reduce compute. there are tradeoffs on latency but big wins on cost.
[05:36] Mark: infra question — if we go Private on-prem, what's rough lead time?
[05:41] Jordan: Private on-prem is longer — typically 6-12 weeks depending on environment and security sign-offs; VPC Private is faster, Dedicated is fastest to get started.
[05:52] Olga: procurement windows may push us to Dedicated first, then Private later.
[05:56] Jordan: that's a common path. ok let's talk pilot design: we propose 1 week of traffic replay or shadow testing plus 3 days of live traffic on Dedicated, with Redwood running parity evals. does that sound reasonable?
[06:10] Ethan: yes, especially if you can run our sample prompts and share comparison metrics.
[06:15] Priya: we'll need: sample prompt sets, golden outputs, definition of pass/fail for evals, and expected QPS/peak to size capacity.
[06:25] Lina: we can export our eval set and metrics, we'll include ROUGE, factuality checks, and a small human-annotated sample for quality.
[06:34] Jordan: perfect. I'll share the pricing tiers and Dedicated sizing matrix after the call. Priya will share benchmark template and past perf sheets where we've compared to OpenAI.
[06:44] Olga: do you have references from other customers who migrated from OpenAI?
[06:48] Jordan: yes — we'll include a short reference list; a couple customers in SaaS and e-comm who moved to Dedicated.
[06:55] Ethan: last thing — any limitations around model licensing? we sometimes use licensed models through OpenAI.
[07:02] Priya: model licensing varies; for proprietary or commercial models hosted only via OpenAI you may need to keep them with OpenAI or get licensing for self-hosting. we can host open weights and some vendor-allowed weights; we'll surface specifics once you share a list.
[07:17] Mark: ok. timeline from here: pricing and benchmark template by next week, then we supply prompts and metrics, then schedule pilot.
[07:25] Jordan: yep. I'll follow up with a calendar invite for the pilot planning meeting.
[07:29] Olga: thanks everyone.
[07:31] Ethan: thanks, talk soon.

[End of transcript — note: auto-transcription had a few mislabels and filler artifacts. Conversation contained technical clarifications on kv cache, kernel selection, quantization, and routing policies.]
